text: A cloud is made of billions of droplets far too small to see one by one.
Each droplet is so tiny and light that rising air holds it up.
A normal fluffy cloud holds around 500 tonnes of water, spread out over a huge space. That's about the weight of 100 elephants, floating over your head.

frames.cap: The Sun warms the sea. Water evaporates. It turns into invisible gas and rises.
High up it's cold. The gas cools and sticks to tiny specks of dust, forming droplets.
Billions of tiny droplets together make a cloud. Each droplet is so light it floats.
Droplets bump and join. When they get heavy enough, they fall as rain.

quiz.prompt: Raindrops are made from much smaller cloud droplets joining together. About how many droplets make one raindrop?

options.t: About a million
About ten
About a thousand

quiz.reveal: About a million. A cloud droplet is around 0.02 mm across and a raindrop about 2 mm, a hundred times wider. Volume grows with the cube, so 100 × 100 × 100 is a million.

d.try: Fill a glass with ice and water and leave it on a table. In a few minutes, tiny drops appear on the outside. They didn't leak through the glass. They are water vapour from the air, cooled by the glass until it turned back into liquid, just as it does to make a cloud.
myth: Raindrops are shaped like teardrops.
Small raindrops are almost perfectly round. Bigger ones get flattened on the bottom as they fall, more like the top half of a burger bun. The very biggest wobble and break apart into smaller drops.
facts: Water in a fluffy cumulus cloud

sec.t:
How can something that heavy float? The trick is that the water is spread very thin. A typical fluffy cumulus cloud might be a kilometre wide, a kilometre long and a kilometre tall. Each cubic metre of it holds only about half a gram of water, about ten drops from an eyedropper.

Each droplet is about 0.02 mm across, thinner than a hair. Droplets that small fall very slowly, so the gentle rising air that builds clouds keeps them aloft. The air around them is heavy too. A cubic kilometre of air weighs far more than the cloud's water, so the cloud is just a slightly misty part of the sky.

Air always carries some water as an invisible gas called water vapour. When air rises, it cools. Cool air can't hold as much vapour, so some of it turns back into liquid, a process called condensation.

But vapour needs something to cling to. Every cloud droplet forms around a speck of [[@earth-weird-red-rain-kerala|dust, sea salt, pollen or smoke]], far too small to see. Without these seeds, clouds would hardly form at all. Scientists have tried [[@sky-cloud-seeding|"seeding" clouds]] by spraying in extra specks, including in experiments in India, but the results are mixed.

Thin clouds look bright white because their droplets scatter all colours of sunlight equally. That's also why clouds are white while the [[@sky-blue|sky is blue]]. Thick clouds full of big droplets let less light through, so from underneath they look grey or almost black. A dark sky means a lot of water overhead.

The biggest rain clouds, called cumulonimbus, can tower more than 12 km high, taller than Mount Everest. They bring downpours, [[@hailstorms-india|hail]] and lightning.

Rain is measured with a simple rain gauge: a funnel and a container that records how deep the water would be if none of it drained away. India's [[@monsoon|monsoon]] brings most of the country's rain in just four months.

Mawsynram and Cherrapunji in [[@meghalaya|Meghalaya]] are among the [[@wettest-place|wettest places]] on Earth, with more than 11 metres of rain in an average year. Once rain lands, it soaks into the ground, runs into rivers or evaporates again, as part of the endless [[@water-cycle|water cycle]].

text: Swirling liquid iron in Earth's [[core|core]] creates a magnetic field all around the planet.
A compass needle is a small magnet. It turns to line up with that field.
The magnetic field also shields us from a stream of particles blasted out by [[@sun-what|the Sun]].

st.prompt: Why does a compass needle point north?

options.t: A giant magnet rock at the North Pole
The whole Earth acts like a magnet
The Pole Star pulls it

st.reveal: Earth's liquid iron outer core swirls around, and that makes the whole planet act like a giant magnet. A compass needle is a tiny magnet, so it lines up with Earth's magnetism.
st.nudge: Lots of people used to think that! But the magnetism comes from deep inside Earth.

d.try: Make a floating compass. Stroke a steel paperclip, straightened out, about 30 times in one direction with a fridge magnet. Lay it on a small leaf or bottle cap floating in a bowl of water. Watch it slowly turn and settle. Check its direction with a phone compass or the setting Sun.
myth: A compass points exactly to the North Pole.

It points to the magnetic north pole, which is hundreds of kilometres from the geographic North Pole and wanders every year. Map makers publish the difference for each place so travellers can correct for it.
facts: swirling liquid iron in Earth's outer core
up to about 50 km a year in recent decades
Last time north and south swapped

sec.t:
About 2,900 km below your feet, Earth's outer core is a churning ocean of liquid iron and nickel, hotter than 4,000 °C. Heat escaping from deeper inside makes the metal rise and sink, a bit like soup bubbling in a pot. Earth's spin twists those currents into spirals.

Moving metal that carries electric currents makes magnetism. So the outer core works like a giant dynamo, the same idea as the generator on some bicycle lights. The result is a magnetic field shaped a lot like the one around a bar [[@magnets-how|magnet]], with one end near each pole.

Every so often, over hundreds of thousands of years, Earth's magnetic field flips. North becomes south, and a compass would point the other way. The last full flip happened about 780,000 years ago.

We know because rocks remember. When lava cools, tiny magnetic minerals inside it line up with the field like frozen compass needles. Lava on the [[@ocean-floor-maps|ocean floor]] shows stripes of normal and flipped magnetism on either side of undersea volcanic ridges. In the 1960s, those stripes helped prove that the sea floor spreads and [[@continental-drift|continents move]], as India did on its long [[@india-drift|journey north]].

The Sun constantly blows out a stream of charged particles called the [[@solar-wind|solar wind]]. Earth's magnetic field steers most of them around the planet. Near the poles, some slip down into the air and make it glow green and red. That glow is the [[@aurora|aurora]]. The same particles can damage [[@satellites-help|satellites]] and disturb radio signals, so space agencies keep a close watch on the Sun.

Mars has almost no magnetic field today. Many scientists think that over billions of years the solar wind stripped away much of its air, which is one reason Mars is so cold and dry.

Many animals [[@pigeons-homing|sense Earth's magnetism]]. Baby loggerhead [[@sea-turtles|sea turtles]] hatch on a beach, swim thousands of kilometres around an ocean, and years later return to nest on the coast where they were born. Scientists think they remember the magnetic "signature" of their home beach. Migrating birds, salmon and some insects seem to use the field too.

People caught on much later. Chinese inventors made the first magnetic compasses for finding the way around 1,000 years ago, and the idea spread to sailors across the Indian Ocean and Europe.

text: The Kuiper Belt (say "KY-per") is a huge, doughnut-shaped region of icy objects beyond the orbit of Neptune. It stretches from about 30 to 50 times Earth's distance from the Sun.

It is filled with frozen leftovers from when the planets formed, about 4.6 billion years ago. Most are small chunks of ice and rock. A few are big enough to be [[@dwarf-planets|dwarf planets]], including Pluto, the largest known.

It is like the [[@asteroid-origin|asteroid belt]] between Mars and Jupiter, but much wider and much more massive, and made mostly of ice instead of rock. Many comets that swing past the Sun every few decades or centuries probably started out here.

options.t: It had to carry out the flyby on its own, without live help from Earth
It had to stop and wait for each command
It made no difference at all

st.reveal: A command from Earth would have taken around six hours to arrive, and the reply another six. So engineers sent the whole flyby plan ahead of time, and New Horizons followed it by itself.

d.try: Make a scale model of the solar system on a long corridor or playground with a teacher. If Earth is 1 step from the Sun, Neptune is 30 steps and the Kuiper Belt runs from about 30 to 50 steps. Place a pebble for each planet and scatter grains of rice for the Kuiper Belt.
myth: The Kuiper Belt is a crowded field of rocks, like in science-fiction films.
It holds a huge number of objects, but they are spread across an enormous region. A spacecraft can cross it without coming anywhere near anything, unless it aims for a target on purpose.
facts: beyond Neptune, about 30 to 50 times Earth's distance from the Sun
icy bodies, rock and frozen gases
1992, by David Jewitt and Jane Luu

sec.t:
After Pluto was discovered in 1930, some astronomers wondered whether it had company. In the 1940s and 1950s, Kenneth Edgeworth in Ireland and Gerard Kuiper in the USA both wrote about small bodies beyond Neptune. Kuiper actually thought any such belt would have been cleared away long ago. The name stuck to him anyway, and some astronomers say "Edgeworth–Kuiper Belt" to share the credit.

For decades, nobody could see anything there. The objects are small, dark and very far away, so they reflect only a sliver of sunlight.

NASA's New Horizons spacecraft flew past [[@pluto|Pluto]] in 2015. Then engineers pointed it at a much smaller target, found by the [[@hubble|Hubble]] Space Telescope only in 2014.

On 1 January 2019, New Horizons flew past it, about 6.6 billion km from Earth. It is the most distant object any spacecraft has visited. The pictures showed two flattened, reddish lumps gently stuck together, about 36 km long in total. It looked a bit like a squashed snowman.

The object was named Arrokoth, meaning "sky" in the Powhatan language of the Native people of the Chesapeake Bay region. Its two lobes probably drifted together very slowly, early in the solar system's history, and have barely changed since.

Out there, the Sun looks like a very bright star, and temperatures are around −230 °C. Nothing melts, and few things crash. So Kuiper Belt objects may be the best-preserved leftovers of the solar system's birth.

Some may have been thrown around by the giant planets long ago. Neptune's largest moon, Triton, orbits backwards, which suggests it was once a Kuiper Belt object captured by Neptune's gravity. Sunlight, the fastest thing there is, takes four to seven hours to reach the Kuiper Belt. A car driving nonstop at 100 km/h would need [[@speed-distance|more than 5,000 years]] just to reach its inner edge.

text: A wing is shaped and tilted so that the air flowing past it gets pushed downward.

Push air down, and the air pushes the wing up. This upward push is called [[lift|lift]]. The faster a plane goes, the more air its wings can turn, and the more lift they make. A big passenger jet needs to reach about 250 to 300 km/h on the runway before its wings can carry its weight.
More speed or more tilt makes more lift, but tilt the wing too much and the air stops flowing smoothly over it. The lift suddenly drops. Pilots call this a stall.

quiz.prompt: Stunt planes at air shows can fly upside down. How do their wings still hold them up?

options.t: The pilot tilts the wing so it still pushes air downwards
They switch on hidden rockets
They can't, they are really falling slowly

quiz.reveal: Lift comes from the wing turning air downwards. Upside down, the pilot raises the plane's nose so the wing meets the air at a tilt that still deflects air towards the ground. Stunt planes often have wings shaped the same on top and bottom to make this easier.

d.try: Stand about a metre in front of a pedestal fan and hold a stiff piece of card flat in the breeze, holding it loosely at one edge. Tilt the front edge up a little and feel the card try to rise. Tilt it more and more. At some point the lift fades and the card just gets shoved backwards. That is a stall.
myth: Air over the top of a wing goes faster because it has to "catch up" with the air underneath at the back.

Nothing makes the air meet up again. Air over the top actually arrives at the back well before the air below. Wings work by turning air downwards, which creates lower pressure above the wing and higher pressure below.

sec.t:
A wing in flight works a bit like a flat hand held up in a strong wind. Tilt your fingers up slightly and the rushing air lifts your hand. The air is being bent downwards, and by Newton's third law, the wing is pushed the other way.

At the same time, the air pressure above the curved wing drops, and the pressure below rises. That difference in pressure is another way of describing the same lift. Both explanations are true, and they fit together. Behind a big jet, you can sometimes see the downwash in clouds or mist, scooped down by the passing wings.

Many books used to say that air over a wing goes faster because it has to "meet up" with the air underneath at the back edge. That's not true. Wind tunnel experiments show air over the top arrives well before the air below. NASA lists the idea as an incorrect theory. The air does speed up over the top, but because of how the wing bends the flow, not because of any meeting.

{{story:cricket-swing}}

Moving flaps on the wings, a rudder on the tail and elevators let pilots climb, turn and slow down. At take-off and landing, extra flaps slide out of the wings to make them bigger and more curved. That gives more lift at low speed, so planes don't need impossibly long runways. On long flights an autopilot does much of the steady flying, while the pilots keep watch and handle take-off, landing and anything unexpected.

Jets cruise about 11 km up, higher than Mount Everest, because the air there is thin. Thin air means less drag, so the plane uses less fuel. Their [[@plane-jet|jet engines]] still find enough air to burn.

In 1903, at [[@wright-to-moon|Kitty Hawk]] in North Carolina, the [[@wright-brothers|Wright brothers]] made the first powered, controlled aeroplane flights. Orville was at the controls while Wilbur ran alongside, steadying the wing. The very first flight lasted 12 seconds and covered about 37 m, less than the wingspan of a modern jumbo jet. They had watched birds closely, especially how they [[@how-birds-fly|twist their wings]] to turn, and copied the idea by twisting their own wings with wires.

On 15 October 1932, J.R.D. Tata flew a small single-engine plane from Karachi to Bombay, now Mumbai, via Ahmedabad, carrying mail. It was the first flight of Tata's airmail service. His service grew into Tata Airlines, which later became Air India. Today India is one of the world's busiest flying nations, and every one of those flights stays up for the same reason as the Wrights' wooden flyer.

text: Every autumn, millions of monarch butterflies fly from Canada and the eastern USA to a few mountain forests in central [[@mexico|Mexico]], up to 4,800 km away. None of them has been there before. They steer using the Sun as a compass, checked against a [[@jet-lag|body clock]] in their antennae.

The Sun moves across the sky during the day, so a butterfly needs to know the time to use it. The antennae clock keeps track, and the monarch adjusts its heading. On cloudy days, monarchs may also sense [[@earth-magnet|Earth's magnetic field]]. Exactly how they find the same small patches of forest, year after year, is still a mystery.

st.prompt: What do monarchs use as their main compass?

options.t: The Sun
The smell of the sea
Following birds

st.reveal: Monarchs use the Sun's position, corrected by a body clock in their antennae, to keep heading south-west. They may also sense Earth's magnetic field on cloudy days.

src: Reppert S.M. & de Roode J.C. (2018) Demystifying monarch butterfly migration. Current Biology 28.

myth: If you touch a butterfly's wings, it will never fly again.
Wings are covered in tiny scales that rub off like dust, but a butterfly can usually still fly after a gentle touch. Rough handling can tear the wings, though, so it is kindest to look and not touch.
facts: mountain fir forests in central Mexico

sec.t:
For decades, nobody outside central Mexico knew where the monarchs went. A Canadian scientist, Fred Urquhart, spent years putting tiny tags on butterflies and asking volunteers to report them. Each tag was a tiny sticker pressed onto a wing, printed with a number and an address to write to. In 1975, two of his helpers, Ken Brugger and Catalina Aguado, found the winter colony on a mountain in Mexico. Local people had known about the butterflies for a long time.

The fir forests there are high, cool and damp. The butterflies cluster on the trees in their millions, turning branches orange. Today the area is protected as the Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve, a UNESCO [[@unesco-sites|World Heritage]] Site since 2008.

Monarchs that live west of the [[@rocky-mountains|Rocky Mountains]] take a shorter route. Most spend the winter in groves of trees along the coast of California, in towns such as Pacific Grove. Volunteers count them every year around [[@thanksgiving|Thanksgiving]].

Their numbers have swung wildly. In 2020 the volunteers found fewer than 2,000 butterflies, a tiny fraction of the millions counted in the 1980s. The next year they counted about 2.5 lakh (250,000). Scientists are still working out why numbers jumped so quickly, and whether it will last. In 2024 the count fell again, to about 9,000, and in 2025 it was only a little higher, at about 12,000.

sec.h: A bitter meal and a warning
sec.t:
Monarch caterpillars eat only milkweed, a plant with bitter poisons in its sap. The caterpillars store the poison, and adult monarchs taste bad to most birds. Their bright orange wings act as a warning.

Monarch numbers have fallen a lot since the 1990s, partly because milkweed has been cleared from farms and roadsides. In 2024, the US government proposed protecting the monarch as a threatened species, and many families now plant milkweed in gardens and schoolyards.

India has its own relatives of the monarch. The plain tiger butterfly, common in Indian gardens, belongs to the same group. In southern India, huge numbers of tiger and crow butterflies migrate between the Western and Eastern Ghats around the monsoon. Like the falcons in [[@migration|bird migration]], they travel by instinct to places they have never seen.

text: A bubble is a thin skin of soapy water wrapped around some air. That skin is always pulling inwards, trying to shrink, like a stretched balloon. Scientists call this pull [[surface-tension|surface tension]].

The air inside pushes back, so the skin can't shrink to nothing. Instead, it settles into the shape that holds that amount of air using the smallest possible area of skin. That shape is a sphere. A cube or a pyramid with the same amount of air inside would need more skin, so the bubble pulls itself round.

Raindrops tend towards round shapes for the same reason, though air rushing past them as they fall squashes them a bit. Out in space, astronauts have watched blobs of water float as almost perfect spheres.

st.prompt: You dip a wand bent into a square shape into bubble mix and blow. What shape is the bubble that floats away?

options.t: Round
Square
A cube with rounded corners

st.reveal: The film's pull squeezes the air inside into the shape with the smallest possible surface, and that shape is a sphere. The wand only shapes the film while it is attached. Once the bubble breaks free, it rounds itself out.

d.try: Mix half a cup of washing-up liquid with about four cups of water and a spoon of sugar or glycerine, and let it rest for an hour. Bend a pipe cleaner into a square, a triangle and a star, and blow bubbles through each. Then blow two bubbles onto a wet plate so they touch, and look at the wall where they meet.
myth: A square bubble wand makes square bubbles.
The wand shape doesn't matter once the bubble is free. The film always pulls itself into a sphere, because that wraps the trapped air in the least possible skin.
facts: Shape with the least surface for its volume
often less than a thousandth of a millimetre
light reflecting off both sides of the thin film

sec.t:
Plain water has strong surface tension, so strong that a skin of pure water snaps almost as soon as it forms. Soap weakens the pull and spreads it more evenly. Soap molecules have one end that likes water and one end that avoids it, the same trick that lets [[@soap-germs|soap lift dirt]] off your hands. They line up on both sides of the film, making a sandwich: soap, a thin layer of water, then soap again.

The soap also slows down evaporation, so the water in the middle lasts longer. Adding sugar or glycerine to bubble mix helps even more, because it holds on to the water. In 1890, the British scientist Charles Vernon Boys gave famous lectures to children in London about bubbles and later published them as a book, *Soap Bubbles*, still in print today.

A bubble's film is thinner than a human hair, often less than a thousandth of a millimetre. When light hits it, some bounces off the outside surface and some off the inside surface. The two reflections overlap. Depending on how thick the film is, some colours add together and others cancel out.

As the water drains down and evaporates, the film gets thinner and the colours swirl and change. Just before a bubble pops, the top often goes dark, because the film has become too thin to reflect visible colours at all. The colours on an oil spill on a wet road come from the same effect. It's a different trick from the bending of light that makes a [[@rainbow-how|rainbow]].

A bubble pops when its film breaks. [[@gravity-fall|Gravity]] drains the water downwards, so the top gets thinner. Water evaporates into the air. A speck of dust or a dry finger can puncture it in an instant.

That's why bubbles last longer on humid days, when the air is already damp and evaporation is slow. Touch a bubble with a finger wet with bubble mix, and it often survives. Bubble artists use this trick, along with special mixes, to make bubbles as big as a car or to put a child inside one.

text: Inside every vacuum cleaner is an electric motor that spins a fan very fast. The fan throws air out through the back of the machine. That leaves the air inside a little thinner than the air in the room. Scientists say the pressure inside is lower.

Air always flows from where the pressure is higher to where it is lower. So air from the room rushes in through the nozzle to fill the gap, and it carries dust, crumbs and hair with it. Before the air leaves through the back, it passes through a bag or a filter that catches the dirt.
So it isn't really sucking. The room's air is pushing the dirt in.

st.prompt: When a vacuum cleaner picks up a crumb, what is really moving the crumb into the nozzle?

options.t: A pulling force from the motor
The higher air pressure in the room pushing in
Static electricity

st.reveal: The fan pushes air out of the back of the machine, leaving slightly lower pressure inside. The air in the room, which is at higher pressure, rushes in through the nozzle to fill the gap and carries the crumb with it. Air always moves from high pressure to low.

d.try: Drink through a straw and notice what you're doing. Your mouth makes a little space with lower pressure, and the air pressing on the drink's surface pushes the liquid up the straw. Now pinch a tiny hole in the straw and try again. It gets much harder, just like a vacuum cleaner with a leaky hose.
myth: A vacuum cleaner makes a vacuum inside it, a space with no air at all.

The air inside is only a little thinner than the air in the room. That small difference is enough to make a strong rush of air into the nozzle. A true vacuum, like outer space, is something no household machine could make.

sec.t:
All around you, air is pressing on everything. You don't feel it because it presses equally from all sides. When one side has less pressure, things move. [[@wind-blows|Wind]] is air moving from high pressure to low pressure across the countryside. A vacuum cleaner makes a tiny, fast wind into its nozzle.

Your [[@lungs-breathe|lungs]] work the same way. When the muscle under your lungs pulls down, the space inside your chest gets bigger and the pressure drops. Air from outside rushes in. Nobody pulls it.

That's also why a narrow nozzle cleans better than a wide one. The same amount of air has to squeeze through a smaller opening, so it moves faster and grabs more dirt.

In 1907, James Murray Spangler, a cleaner at a department store in Ohio, USA, got coughing fits from the dust stirred up by his carpet sweeper. He built a small electric vacuum from a fan motor, a pillowcase and a broom handle, and patented it in 1908. He sold the rights to a relative's husband, William Hoover. The company did so well that in Britain people still say "hoovering" for vacuuming.

Later, in the 1980s and 1990s, the British inventor James Dyson built a bagless vacuum that spins air in a cone, a cyclone, so dust is flung out to the sides. He said he built more than 5,000 prototypes before it worked well.

Household dust is made of skin flakes, fibres, soil, pollen and tiny creatures called [[@gross-dust-mites|dust mites]]. For people with [[@allergies|allergies]] or asthma, dust can cause sneezing, itchy eyes and wheezing.

Cheap filters let the finest dust blow straight out of the back and into the air. Better vacuums use HEPA filters, which trap tiny particles that a normal filter misses. Today many homes in India and the USA also have small round robot vacuums, which steer around furniture with sensors. They use exactly the same pressure trick as Booth's horse-drawn giant.

text: Street theatre is drama performed in public places, such as street corners, markets, parks, bus stands and factory gates. The audience doesn't buy tickets. People simply stop, gather round and watch, and they are free to walk away.

In India it is often called nukkad natak, a street-corner play. The plays are short, usually 15 to 30 minutes, with few props and no costumes beyond a scarf or a cap. Actors use loud voices, songs, drums and big movements so people at the back can follow. Many plays are about everyday problems, like prices, health, schooling or elections, and they often end by asking the crowd a question.

st.prompt: Why do street theatre actors usually perform in a circle, with the audience all around them?

options.t: There is no stage, so a circle lets everyone see and lets passers-by join in
Sound bounces better in a circle
It is a rule from ancient Greece

st.reveal: In a street there are no seats and no raised stage. A ring of people means everyone gets a view, and newcomers can squeeze in at the edges. Actors turn as they speak so nobody sees only their back.

myth: Street theatre is just amateur acting by people who couldn't get on a real stage.

Many street theatre performers are highly trained, and some famous actors began in street groups. Playing outdoors, with traffic noise and a moving crowd, takes special skills of voice, movement and timing.

sec.t:
A performance usually starts with noise. Actors beat a dholak, clap, sing or shout a slogan until a crowd forms. Then they make a circle and step inside it.

One actor might play three characters in five minutes, swapping a cap for a dupatta to show the change. The group can become a bus, a wall or a crowd with their bodies. There are no lights or speakers, so voices must carry over horns and street sellers. Jokes keep people from drifting off. When it ends, actors often pass around a cloth bag for donations.

Modern street theatre took off in India in the 1970s and 1980s. In 1973 a group of young people in Delhi formed Jana Natya Manch, often called Janam. Its best-known member, the writer and director Safdar Hashmi, wrote plays that were performed at hundreds of street corners and factory gates.

On 1 January 1989, Janam was performing a play called Halla Bol near Delhi when the group was attacked. Safdar Hashmi was badly hurt and died the next day. Two days later, his wife Moloyshree Hashmi and the group returned to the same place and finished the play. Thousands came to watch. Every year since, Janam has gone back to perform there on 1 January.

Because street plays are cheap and go where people already are, they are used to spread ideas. Government departments and charities have used nukkad nataks to explain vaccines, voting, clean water and children's rights. A play in a village square can reach people who never read posters or watch adverts.

That power is also why street theatre can be controversial. Plays sometimes criticise powerful people. In a [[@democracy-india|democracy]], the right to perform such plays is linked to [[@free-speech|free speech]], though in many places groups still need police permission to perform in public.

In the United States, the Bread and Puppet Theater began in New York in 1963 and later moved to a farm in Vermont. It is known for giant [[@puppetry|puppets]], some taller than a house, carried through streets in parades. Its founders also handed out fresh bread they had baked to the audience.

The San Francisco Mime Troupe, founded in 1959, has given free shows in the city's parks since 1962. Like a nukkad natak, its plays are funny, loud and about things in the news.

A good street play pulls you in because it is happening right in front of you, in your own lane. You can see the actors sweat. The [[@drums|drums]] are real, the jokes are about your town, and the person laughing next to you might be your neighbour. For a few minutes, an ordinary corner becomes a [[@theatre|theatre]].

text: Tanjore paintings shine because they use real gold. Artists press thin sheets of gold leaf onto raised parts of the picture: a god's crown, jewellery, the pillars of a temple arch. Then they add glittering glass beads and coloured stones.

The style comes from Thanjavur (once called Tanjore), [[@tamil-nadu-temples|a temple town]] in Tamil Nadu. These paintings were made to be worshipped as well as admired. In a dim prayer room, lit by an oil lamp, the gold glows and seems to flicker. That was the point. The god in the picture looks as if it is shining with its own light.

st.prompt: Why do the gold parts of a Tanjore painting stand out from the board, like a little sculpture?

options.t: The painter builds them up with a thick paste before adding gold
The gold is melted and poured on in drops

st.reveal: The artist pipes or presses a paste of chalk and glue onto the jewellery, crowns and pillars, building them up in layers. When it dries, gold leaf is laid on top, so the gold catches light from every side.

sec.h: A town of temples and kings
sec.t:
Thanjavur had been a great centre of art since the [[@cholas|Cholas]] built the Brihadeeswarar temple there about a thousand years ago. The painting style we call Tanjore grew much later, from the 1600s to the 1800s. By then Thanjavur was ruled by a [[@marathas|Maratha royal family]], and kings like Serfoji II supported musicians, scholars and painters.

Many of the painters came from families of craftsmen who had worked on temples and palaces for generations. They painted Hindu gods and goddesses, saints and scenes from sacred stories, for temples and for the prayer rooms of wealthy homes.

Gold has a special property that paint does not. It barely reacts with air or water, so it does not rust or turn dark the way silver and copper do. That is why gold coins dug up after many centuries can still gleam.

Gold can also be hammered extraordinarily thin. Craftsmen beat it between layers of leather or paper until a lump the size of a pea spreads across a large sheet. A little gold covers a lot of painting, and it reflects lamplight beautifully.

Tanjore figures are easy to recognise. Faces are round and gentle, with large, almond-shaped eyes. The main god sits in the centre, much larger than the people and animals around it, because size shows importance.

The most loved subject is Krishna as a chubby baby, often holding a ball of butter. Colours are flat and strong: deep red, green, blue and white, with dark outlines. Unlike the shading in a [[@raja-ravi-varma|Raja Ravi Varma]] painting, there is little attempt to look like real life. The aim is to feel holy.

Families in and around Thanjavur still make these paintings. "Thanjavur Paintings" is protected by a geographical indication, a legal label that says real ones must come from the region and follow the traditional method. Today many go into homes as gifts at weddings or housewarmings, often hung where a family prays, sometimes beside a small [[@bronze-casting|bronze]] image cast in the same part of Tamil Nadu.

text: Superstitions come from the way the [[@brain-works|human brain]] hunts for patterns. If something good or bad happens right after you do something, your brain tends to link the two, even if it was pure chance. Once people share that belief, it gets passed on through families, stories and cultures.

Many superstitions also have old roots. Some come from ancient religious ideas, some from practical warnings, and some from old explanations of the world before science. Others started as jokes and stuck. People keep them because they are comforting. Doing a small ritual gives a feeling of control when life feels uncertain, like before an exam, a match or a journey.

st.prompt: In Skinner's 1948 experiment, the pigeons got food at fixed times, whatever they did. What happened?

options.t: Each pigeon repeated whatever it happened to be doing when food last arrived
The pigeons sat still and waited calmly

st.reveal: One pigeon spun in circles, another bobbed its head and another thrust its head into a corner. Each had been doing that when food happened to appear, and it kept repeating the action as if it caused the food. Skinner called this superstition.

myth: Only people who don't know science are superstitious.

Superstitions are common among all kinds of people, including scientists, doctors, pilots and sports stars. They come from the way every human brain looks for patterns and tries to feel in control, especially when stakes are high.

sec.t:
In 1948, the American psychologist B. F. Skinner put hungry [[@pigeons-homing|pigeons]], birds better known for finding their way home, in boxes. A machine dropped food in every 15 seconds, no matter what the birds did.

After a few days, most of the pigeons had invented strange rituals. One turned in circles before each feed. Another bobbed its head up and down. Each was repeating whatever it had been doing when the food happened to arrive. Skinner called this "superstition". Humans do something similar when they wear the same socks for every match because they once won wearing them.

sec.h: A black cat and a broken mirror
sec.t:
The black cat superstition is very old. In medieval Europe, black cats were linked with witches, and some people feared them. In India, many people believe a black cat crossing your path means bad luck, and some wait for someone else to cross first.

Yet in parts of Britain and in Japan, black cats have been seen as lucky. Sailors' families in England once kept them to bring their men home safely.

The broken mirror idea is often traced back to the ancient Romans, who thought a mirror held a piece of your soul. Some say the seven years of bad luck came from a belief that life renewed itself every seven years.

sec.h: Lemons, chillies and the evil eye
sec.t:
Walk past shops in many Indian towns and you will see a lemon and seven green chillies hung on a string over the door. This is *nimbu-mirchi*, meant to protect against *nazar*, the evil eye. One popular explanation is that the sour and spicy smell keeps away bad luck, or the goddess of misfortune, Alakshmi.

Belief in the evil eye is found from India to Turkey, Greece and Mexico. In Türkiye, people hang blue glass eyes called *nazar boncuğu*. In India, parents may put a small black dot of kajal on a baby's cheek.

Sports stars are famous for superstitions. Some cricketers always put on their left pad first, and the list of [[@sport-weird|strange sporting habits]] is long. Others carry a red handkerchief or refuse to change their bat during a winning streak. Tennis players bounce the ball a set number of times before serving.

Psychologists think such rituals can help a little. They don't change luck, but they can calm nerves and help players focus. A 2010 study in Germany found that people who were told their golf ball was "lucky" sank more putts. Whether that result holds up is still debated, as other teams could not always repeat it.

The best way to test a superstition is to keep careful records, an idea from [[@probability|probability]]. If Friday the 13th is unlucky, there should be more accidents on those days than on other Fridays. When researchers check, they usually find no real difference.

But knowing that doesn't always stop people. Plenty of tall buildings still skip floor 13, just as hotels in China skip floor 4. Numbers have their own long list of [[@life-lucky-numbers|lucky and unlucky meanings]], and many of them started in the same place: a brain trying to find order in a world full of chance.

text: You're on a game show. There are three closed doors. Behind one is a car, and behind the other two are goats. You choose a door, say door 1. The host, who knows what is behind each door, opens one of the other doors, say door 3, to show a goat. Then he asks: do you want to switch to door 2?
You should switch. Sticking wins the car only 1 time in 3. Switching wins 2 times in 3. Almost everyone's gut says it's 50–50, and almost everyone's gut is wrong.

st.prompt: You pick door 1. The host, who knows where the car is, opens door 3 to show a goat. Should you switch to door 2?

options.t: Yes, switching wins 2 times out of 3
It makes no difference, it's 50–50
No, sticking is safer

st.reveal: Your first pick had a 1 in 3 chance. The host's choice gives you no new information about your door, but it does tell you about the others. So the 2 in 3 chance that the car was behind "one of the other doors" now rests on the single door left.

d.try: Play it with a friend using three cups and a coin. Your friend hides the coin and, after you pick, lifts an empty cup you didn't choose. Play 30 rounds where you always stick and 30 where you always switch, and count your wins. Switching should win about twice as often.
myth: Once two doors are left, each has an equal 50–50 chance.

sec.t:
When you first pick, you have a 1 in 3 chance of being right. That means there is a 2 in 3 chance the car is behind one of the other two doors.

Now the host steps in. He will always open a door with a goat, never the car, and never your door. So he isn't guessing. He is using what he knows to remove a loser from the other two.

The 2 in 3 chance that belonged to "the other doors" doesn't vanish. It all moves onto the one door he left shut.

Still not convinced? Most people aren't. Try making it bigger.

Picture 100 doors, with one car. You pick door 1. The host, who knows where the car is, opens 98 other doors, all with goats. Only your door and door 74 are left.

Do you really think your first blind guess, out of 100, was right? Or did the host just carefully avoid one particular door? Switching now wins 99 times out of 100. The three-door game is the same idea, only smaller.

sec.h: The column that caused an uproar
sec.t:
The puzzle is named after Monty Hall, host of the American TV show *Let's Make a Deal*, which began in 1963. A statistician named Steve Selvin first wrote it up as a puzzle in 1975.

In 1990, a reader sent it to Marilyn vos Savant, who wrote a popular question-and-answer column in *Parade* magazine. She said to switch. Thousands of letters poured in saying she was wrong. Many came from people with maths doctorates. Some were rude.

She was right. Teachers across the USA ran the game in classrooms, and the results kept matching her answer. One of the 20th century's greatest mathematicians, Paul Erdős, is said to have stayed unconvinced until he saw a computer simulation.

In 2010, two American psychologists tested pigeons on a version of the game, using lit-up keys instead of doors and food instead of a car.

At first the birds chose randomly. But over many rounds, they learned that switching paid off, and they switched almost every time. University students playing the same game kept sticking far more often. The pigeons didn't think about it. They just counted what worked, which is something our clever human brains struggle to do, as you'll see in why your [[@brain-works|brain gets chances wrong]].

Our brains like simple stories. Two doors left? Must be half and half. We also hate the feeling of switching away from the right answer, more than we hate sticking with a wrong one.

Those habits are useful in everyday life, but [[@probability|probability]] often rewards cold counting over instinct. The puzzle is now a favourite in maths lessons and computer science courses around the world.

The trick only works if the rules are fixed: the host knows where the car is, always opens a goat door, and always offers the switch. If he opens a door at random and happens to show a goat, the chances really do become 50–50.

That is a big lesson hiding in a small game. In [[@probability|probability]], knowing why something happened matters as much as what happened. And if this puzzle bends your brain, wait until you meet the [[@puzzle-birthday|birthday puzzle]], where a class of just 23 children is more likely than not to have a shared birthday.

text: Cartoon voices are made by voice actors, people trained to bring characters to life using only their voices. They stand in soundproof rooms in front of a microphone and perform lines again and again until the director is happy.

Many voice actors play several characters in the same show. Some keep a role for decades. A good one can sound like a squeaky mouse in one moment and a booming dragon the next, without any computer tricks. They have to act with everything except their face and body, since nobody will see them.

st.reveal: In the USA, voices are usually recorded first, so animators can match mouths and expressions to the actor's performance. Japanese anime often works the other way round, with actors recording to finished or nearly finished scenes.

sec.h: The man of a thousand voices
sec.t:
The most famous voice actor of all may be Mel Blanc. Starting in the 1930s, he voiced Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Porky Pig, Tweety, Sylvester and many more for the Looney Tunes cartoons. He was nicknamed "The Man of a Thousand Voices".

For Porky Pig's stutter and Daffy's spluttering lisp, Blanc built each voice from small habits of the mouth and throat. When he died in 1989, his family had his gravestone carved with Porky Pig's famous last line, "That's All Folks".

Even Mickey Mouse began this way. In 1928, Walt Disney himself squeaked Mickey's first words, and he kept the role for almost 20 years.

sec.h: Bending one throat into many characters
sec.t:
Every voice starts in the [[larynx|larynx]], the voice box in your throat, where two small folds vibrate. Voice actors change the speed of those vibrations to go higher or lower. They also shape the sound with the tongue, lips and nose. Squeezing sound through the nose makes a whiny voice. Opening the throat wide makes a deep one.

Long sessions can strain the voice, especially for screaming monsters or gravelly villains. So actors warm up like singers, drink lots of water and save the loudest scenes for the end of the day. A cartoon series can run for hundreds of episodes, so an actor must be able to find exactly the same voice years later.

When cartoons travel to India, a new team of actors records the characters in Hindi, Tamil, Telugu and other languages. This is [[@dubbing-subtitles|dubbing]]. The new actors must match the original mouth movements and timing, and often add local jokes. For the 2019 Hindi version of *The Lion King*, film star Shah Rukh Khan voiced Mufasa, and his son Aryan voiced the grown-up Simba.

Some voices never change. [[@pokemon|Pikachu]] says only its own name, in different tones and moods, so the Japanese actor Ikue Ōtani's voice is used around the world. Homer Simpson has sounded the same since 1987, because Dan Castellaneta has voiced him the whole time, along with dozens of other characters in the same show.

Indian studios now make their own hits, with Indian actors voicing heroes like [[@chhota-bheem|Chhota Bheem]] from the very start. And voices are only half the soundtrack. The crunch of a punch in a cartoon is often made by someone snapping celery or slapping a wet towel. That is a whole hidden job, explored in [[@behind-sound-effects|sound effects]].

text: A few months before every Olympic Games, the flame is lit among the ruins of [[@ancient-olympia|ancient Olympia]] in Greece. A woman playing a high priestess holds a torch inside a curved mirror that focuses sunlight until it bursts into flame.

From there, the flame travels to the host city in a relay. Thousands of torchbearers carry it a short stretch each, passing the fire from torch to torch. When roads run out, it goes by boat, plane, train, horse or canoe. At the opening ceremony, the last torchbearer lights a big cauldron, which burns until the Games end.

st.reveal: A performer dressed as an ancient priestess holds a torch at the centre of a curved, bowl-shaped mirror. The mirror focuses the Sun's rays onto one spot until the torch catches fire. If it's cloudy, they use a backup flame lit at a rehearsal.

sec.h: Not as ancient as it looks

sec.t:
The torch has to keep burning in wind and rain, so modern torches are clever bits of engineering. Most burn a gas such as propane, stored in a small tank in the handle. Designers test them in wind tunnels and under fake rainstorms.

Flames still go out sometimes. In 1976, a rainstorm put out the cauldron in Montreal during the Games, and a worker relit it with a cigarette lighter. Officials quickly put that out and relit it properly from a backup flame. Backups travel everywhere with the relay, burning inside miners' safety lamps, so a lost flame can always be replaced with the "real" one.

That 1976 flame crossed the ocean in the strangest way of all. In Athens, a sensor turned the flame into electronic pulses. A satellite sent them to Ottawa, Canada, where they triggered a laser that lit a new torch.

Other trips are just as odd. For Sydney 2000, a diver carried a special flare-like torch underwater along the Great Barrier Reef. For Beijing 2008, climbers took a flame to the top of Everest. Before the 2014 Sochi Games, astronauts took a torch to the International Space Station and on a spacewalk, but unlit. An open flame on a [[@space-station|space station]] would be far too dangerous.

sec.h: A flame on a sailing ship
sec.t:
For Paris 2024, the flame left Greece aboard the Belem, a three-masted sailing ship built in 1896. It sailed into Marseille, the French city founded by Greek settlers about 2,600 years ago, a neat link between the two countries. Then it toured France and its overseas territories, including islands in the Caribbean and the Pacific.

The next Summer Games, in Los Angeles in 2028, will bring the relay back to the USA. Los Angeles hosted in 1932 and 1984 too.

The Olympic torch relay for Beijing 2008 passed through New Delhi on a shortened, heavily guarded route because of protests. India has started its own torch traditions too. In 2022, a torch relay was held for the first time for the Chess Olympiad, beginning in Delhi and visiting 75 cities before the event in Chennai.

Every relay is a reminder of how far a small flame can travel when enough people pass it on. And the story of how humans first learned to control [[@fire-burns|fire]] is older than any Olympics.

text: Stand-up comedy is one person on a stage, usually with a microphone, trying to make an audience laugh. There's no costume or set, just the comedian talking about everyday life, family, school, food or anything else that seems a bit ridiculous when you look closely.

It looks relaxed, but most of it is planned. Comedians write jokes, try them at small shows, notice which lines get [[@laughter|laughter]], and rewrite the ones that don't. They practise timing, pauses and faces until a ten-minute set feels like a chat with friends.

st.reveal: The psychologist Robert Provine found that most laughter happens in ordinary conversation, often after lines that aren't funny at all. Laughter is mainly a social signal, which is why a comedy club full of people laughs more than one person watching alone.

d.try: Write a three-line joke about something that happened at school or at home. Tell it to two different people, changing only one thing, like the order of words or the length of the pause before the last line. Notice which version gets the bigger laugh.
myth: Stand-up comedians make up their jokes on the spot.
Most stand-up is carefully written, tested on audiences and rehearsed. Comedians may chat with the crowd and add new lines, but quick-fire making-up is a different art called improv.
facts: one person, a microphone and an audience
vaudeville stage shows, from the late 1800s

sec.t:
Most jokes have two parts. The set-up gives the audience a picture and makes them expect something. The punchline then breaks that expectation in a surprising way.

Researchers think we laugh partly because our [[@brain-works|brain]] suddenly has to switch from one meaning to another. A [[@riddles|riddle]] works in a similar way: you are led down one path, then find the answer was somewhere else.

{{story:laughter}}

Comedians also use "callbacks", where a joke from early in the set returns later with a twist. Audiences love catching the reference.

The same words can get a big laugh or silence, depending on how they're said. A pause before the punchline lets tension build. Saying the last word too fast, or too slowly, can kill the joke.

Comedians learn this by performing again and again. Open mic nights, where anyone can sign up for a few minutes on stage, are their testing ground. A comedian might try a new joke twenty times, cutting a word here or adding a look there, before it works every night.

When a set goes badly, comedians say they "bombed". When it goes brilliantly, they "killed". Even famous comedians bomb sometimes, especially when testing new material, and most say it's the only way to find out what works.

In the USA, comic monologues were part of vaudeville, travelling variety shows of the late 1800s and early 1900s, with singers, jugglers and comedians on one bill. Later, comedians told jokes on radio and then on TV talk shows. From the 1970s, comedy clubs opened in many American cities.

India has its own old traditions of comic performance. In a hasya kavi sammelan, poets recite funny poems to an audience, poking fun at politics, marriage and daily life. Comic actors like Johnny Lever performed mimicry and stand-up long before English-language comedy clubs appeared.

In the 2010s, stand-up grew quickly in Indian cities like Mumbai, Delhi and Bengaluru. Comedians performed in cafés and small clubs, then posted their sets on [[@youtube|YouTube]], where some videos reached millions of viewers.

Many comedians perform in Hindi, Tamil, Marathi, Gujarati or a mix of languages. Jokes about Indian parents, exams, traffic and family weddings travel well, because so many people recognise them.

Comedy often pokes at uncomfortable subjects, like politics or religion. That can make people think, and sometimes it upsets them. In India, the USA and many other countries, comedians have faced complaints, cancelled shows or even court cases over jokes.

People disagree about where the lines should be. Some say comedians must be free to mock the powerful. Others say jokes can hurt real people. These arguments are part of a wider debate about [[@free-speech|free speech]] that goes back centuries.

text: Tennis scoring goes love, 15, 30, 40, game, because of habits that grew up in France around 600 years ago. The most popular explanation is a clock. Scorers may have used a clock face with a hand moving a quarter of the way round, to 15, 30 and 45, for each point. The game ended when the hand reached 60.

Over time 45 was shortened to 40, perhaps because it was quicker to say. Nobody wrote the reasons down, so this is a good guess, not a certain answer. The word "love" for zero is even more mysterious.

Draw

st.reveal: Most historians link deuce to the French "à deux", meaning "at two". From 40–40, a player must win two points in a row to take the game.

sec.h: A game played with the palm

sec.t:
From 40–40, a player must win two points in a row. This score is called deuce, probably from the French "à deux", "at two". The player one point ahead has the advantage.

Zero is called love. One story says it comes from "l'oeuf", the French word for egg, because an egg looks like a zero. Most experts find the "nothing" explanation more convincing: to play for love was to play for no reward. Either way, scoring like this turns each game into a mini-drama, because you can be one point from losing and still come back. If the clock theory is right, tennis is one more thing shaped by the old habit of [[@time-measure|counting time]] in sixties.

In 1874 a British army officer, Walter Clopton Wingfield, patented an outdoor game for garden lawns. He gave it the Greek name "sphairistike", which almost nobody could pronounce. People simply called it lawn tennis.

In 1877 the All England Croquet Club in Wimbledon, [[@london|London]], held a lawn tennis tournament to raise money for a new roller for its croquet lawns. About 200 people watched the final. Wimbledon is now the oldest tennis tournament in the world.

Long games were always a risk with this scoring, because a set could go on and on. At Wimbledon in 2010, John Isner of the USA and Nicolas Mahut of France played for 11 hours and 5 minutes over three days. The last set ended 70–68, and the electronic scoreboard stopped working at 47–47.

Tie-breaks, which end a set at 6–6 with a quick count of points, were introduced in the 1970s. In 2022, all four [[@tennis-grand-slams|Grand Slams]] agreed to use a tie-break in the final set too.

India has a proud tennis history. Ramanathan Krishnan reached the Wimbledon semi-finals in 1960 and 1961. Vijay Amritraj was one of the world's top players in the 1970s and 1980s.

At the 1996 Atlanta [[@olympics|Olympics]], Leander Paes won a bronze medal in singles. With Mahesh Bhupathi and others he won many Grand Slam doubles titles. Sania Mirza became India's most successful woman player, winning six Grand Slam doubles and mixed-doubles titles. [[@sports-science|Sports scientists]] now measure serves at over 250 km/h, more than twice a cheetah's top speed, but the score is still called in a language from a medieval French hall.

text: A calculator turns every number you type into [[@binary-code|binary]], a code that uses only 0s and 1s. Inside is a tiny chip containing thousands of electronic switches arranged into circuits called [[@logic|logic]] gates. Some circuits are wired to add two binary numbers. Everything else is built from that.

To subtract, the calculator uses a clever trick that turns subtraction into a kind of addition. To multiply, it adds and shifts numbers along, the way you multiply on paper by writing rows and adding them. To divide, it repeatedly subtracts. For [[@square-roots|square roots]] and trickier functions, it follows step-by-step recipes, called [[@algorithms|algorithms]], that home in on the answer. When it's done, it turns the binary back into ordinary digits on the screen.

st.prompt: You type 2 + 3 × 4 = into a simple shop calculator. What answer does it usually show?
st.reveal: Many simple calculators work out each step as you type, so they do 2 + 3 = 5 first, then 5 × 4 = 20. Scientific calculators follow the rule that multiplication comes before addition, so they give 14. Both are doing exactly what they were built to do.

d.try: Multiply like a calculator. Work out 13 × 5 using only adding and doubling. Double 13 to get 26, double again to get 52 (that is 13 × 4), then add one more 13 to get 65. Calculators break hard sums into steps like these, only in binary and millions of times faster.
myth: A calculator's answer is always exactly right.

Calculators follow their own rules and limits. Simple and scientific calculators can give different answers for the same keys, and because they store only a limited number of digits, answers like 1 ÷ 3 × 3 may come out as 0.9999999 instead of 1.

sec.t:
People have used tools to help with sums for thousands of years. The [[@abacus|abacus]], with beads on rods, was used in ancient [[@mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], China, Rome and India, and skilled users can still beat a calculator on some sums.

In the 1640s, a French teenager named Blaise Pascal built a machine of [[@gears|gears and wheels]] to help his father, a tax official, add long columns of numbers. Turning one wheel a full circle nudged the next wheel along by one, just like carrying a digit. Only a small number of Pascalines were ever made, because each was hard to build and costly. A few decades later, the German mathematician Gottfried Leibniz built a machine that could also multiply.

In the 1820s, Charles Babbage designed huge calculating engines made of thousands of brass parts. He never finished them. In 1991, the Science Museum in London built his Difference Engine No. 2 from his drawings, and it worked perfectly.

For over a century after Babbage, mechanical calculators clattered in offices, and they were heavy and noisy. The first electronic calculators in the 1960s were the size of a typewriter. Then engineers learned to fit many circuits onto one [[@chips-silicon|silicon chip]].

In 1969, the Japanese company Busicom asked a young American firm called Intel to design chips for a new desktop calculator. Intel's engineers came up with a single general-purpose chip that could be programmed to do many jobs. It became the Intel 4004, released in 1971, the first microprocessor sold commercially. The same idea now powers every phone and computer.

By the late 1970s, pocket calculators had become cheap enough to turn up in schoolbags around the world.

{{story:abacus}}

How can switches add? In binary, 0 + 0 = 0, 0 + 1 = 1 and 1 + 1 = 10, which means "write 0, carry 1". A small circuit of logic gates can be built to follow exactly these rules for one column. Line up many such circuits, each passing its carry to the next, and you can add long numbers.

Multiplying 13 by 5 might be done by adding 13 to itself in clever steps, using doubling, which in binary simply means shifting every digit one place to the left. The chip does this so fast that the answer seems to appear the instant you press "=".

Some people can do sums at astonishing speed. In 1980, at Imperial College London, the Indian mathematician [[@shakuntala-devi|Shakuntala Devi]] was given two 13-digit numbers chosen by a computer. She multiplied them in her head in 28 seconds, a feat recorded by [[@world-records|Guinness World Records]].

Methods like [[@vedic-maths|Vedic maths]] also teach [[@maths-shortcuts-indian|shortcuts for mental arithmetic]]. But for most of us, the little machine of switches is faster, as long as we remember to check that its answer makes sense.

text: Maharaja Ranjit Singh was the founder of the Sikh Empire, which ruled Punjab and the lands around it in the early 1800s. Born in 1780, he took control of the city of Lahore in 1799, when he was just 19, and was proclaimed Maharaja of [[@punjab|Punjab]] in 1801.

Over the next four decades he united the quarrelling Sikh groups, called misls, and conquered Multan, [[@kashmir|Kashmir]] and Peshawar. He built one of the strongest armies in Asia, kept the British at a distance through a treaty and ran a court where people of many faiths served. Within ten years of his death in 1839, his empire had fallen to the British.

myth: Ranjit Singh's court was only for Sikhs.
His ministers and generals included Hindus, Muslims, Sikhs and even Europeans. His foreign minister, Fakir Azizuddin, was a Muslim, and he gave gifts to mosques and temples as well as gurdwaras.

sec.t:
Ranjit Singh was born in Gujranwala, in today's Pakistan, the son of the leader of one of the Sikh misls. As a small child he caught smallpox, which left his face scarred and blinded his left eye. He never learned to read or write.

His father died when he was about ten. Ranjit Singh soon proved a sharp leader. In 1799 he rode into Lahore, which had been squabbled over by several chiefs, and its people welcomed him. Lahore became his capital.

sec.h: An army trained by Napoleon's men
sec.t:
Ranjit Singh wanted an army that could match the British. He hired European officers, including Jean-Baptiste Ventura from Italy and Jean-François Allard from France, who had fought in the armies of [[@napoleon|Napoleon]].

They trained his infantry to march and fight in disciplined lines, with modern cannon and uniforms. The army, called the Fauj-i-Khas for its best units, became one of the most powerful forces in Asia. In 1809 he signed the Treaty of Amritsar with the British [[@east-india-company|East India Company]], agreeing that the Sutlej river would be the border between them. Both sides kept that promise while he lived.

sec.h: Gold, a diamond and many faiths
sec.t:
Ranjit Singh paid to cover the upper floors of the Harmandir Sahib in [[@amritsar|Amritsar]] with gilded copper, giving it the name the Golden Temple. He also gave gold for the Kashi Vishwanath temple in Varanasi.

In 1813 he obtained the Koh-i-Noor diamond from Shah Shuja, an exiled ruler of Afghanistan who had taken shelter in Lahore. Ranjit Singh wore it in an armband.

His court mixed faiths and backgrounds. Fakir Azizuddin, a Muslim, was his foreign minister. Dogra Hindu brothers held top posts, and Europeans commanded troops. In 2020, readers of a BBC history magazine voted him the greatest leader of all time, ahead of figures like Abraham Lincoln.

Ranjit Singh, often called Sher-e-Punjab, the Lion of Punjab, died in Lahore in 1839. Without him, his heirs and generals fought each other, and several rulers came and went in a few years.

The British fought two wars with the Sikh army in 1845–46 and 1848–49, and in 1849 they took over Punjab. The last Maharaja, Duleep Singh, was a boy of ten. He was sent to Britain, and the Koh-i-Noor was given to Queen Victoria. It is now part of the [[@london-tower|British Crown Jewels]] in London. Ranjit Singh's memorial, his samadhi, still stands in Lahore beside the great Badshahi Mosque.

text: The Charminar is a huge stone monument in the old city of [[@hyderabad|Hyderabad]], in Telangana. Its name means "four minarets", after the tall towers that rise from its four corners. Sultan Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah built it in 1591.

The building is a square, about 20 m on each side, with a giant arch opening onto each of four streets. It stands about 56 m tall, roughly as high as an 18-storey block of flats. On the top floor is a small mosque. Four hundred years later, it is the picture most people think of when they hear the word Hyderabad.

st.reveal: The top floor holds a small mosque, set on the western side so that people pray facing Mecca. The flat roof around it was also a place to look out over the new city.

n.certNote: Historians agree on who built the Charminar and when. Why it was built is less certain. The story that it marks the end of a plague is popular, but there is no record from the time that proves it.

myth: A secret tunnel runs from the Charminar to Golconda Fort, about 8 km away.
People have told this story for centuries, but no such tunnel has ever been found. Golconda does have clever acoustics and water channels, which may have helped the legend grow.

sec.h: A new city for a new capital
sec.t:
The Qutb Shahi kings first ruled from Golconda, a fort on a granite hill. By the late 1500s Golconda was crowded and short of water. Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah, the fifth sultan, decided to build a new city across the river Musi.

The Charminar was its centrepiece. Four wide roads ran out from its arches towards the four directions, with markets, palaces and gardens laid out along them. In a sense, the city grew outwards from this one building. Muhammad Quli was also a poet who wrote in Dakhni, Telugu and Persian. He ruled for more than 30 years, from 1580 to 1612, and many buildings in old Hyderabad date from his reign. He is often said to have prayed for his new city to be filled with people like a river is filled with fish.

The Charminar is built from granite and limestone, held together with mortar that contained crushed marble. Its walls were covered in lime plaster and decorated with flowers, arches and balconies. Inside each minaret, a narrow staircase of about 149 steps winds up to the top.

The four arches are each about 11 m wide. Above them, two floors of smaller arches run around all four sides. The design mixes Persian ideas with the craftsmanship of the Deccan. Like the [[@qutub-minar|Qutub Minar]] in Delhi, the tall towers were meant to be seen from far away.

In 1889, clocks were added on all four sides. They still keep the time for the streets below.

The Charminar has never been a quiet museum. Lanes packed with shops crowd up to its base. Laad Bazaar, just to the west, has sold glittering lac bangles for centuries, the kind of [[@indian-jewellery|jewellery]] brides still buy there. Pearl sellers line the nearby roads, a reminder that Hyderabad was once a great trading centre for pearls.

Next door stands the Mecca Masjid, one of the largest mosques in India, begun by a later Qutb Shahi king. In the evenings, especially during Ramzan, the area fills with stalls selling haleem and [[@biryani|biryani]].

The Charminar has been worn down by traffic smoke, rain and time. The Archaeological Survey of India looks after it, and restorers have repaired its plaster and minarets several times. Cars are now kept further from its base than they once were, to protect the old stone.

text: Thrissur Pooram is one of Kerala's most spectacular temple festivals, held each year in Thrissur in April or May. It brings together about ten temples from around the city. Their processions of decorated elephants, drummers and musicians gather on the vast grounds around the Vadakkunnathan temple, dedicated to Shiva.

The highlights are huge drum and horn performances, the famous umbrella contest called *kudamattam* and a giant fireworks display in the early morning. Lakhs of people from across Kerala and beyond come to watch, and the whole city becomes one big stage for a day and a half.

sec.h: A festival born from a rainy day
sec.t:
Kerala has many poorams, temple festivals held in the month of Medam. Before 1798, temples from Thrissur went to a big pooram in nearby Arattupuzha. That year, heavy rain delayed them, and they arrived late. They were not allowed to join.

The ruler of Kochi, Raja Rama Varma, known as Sakthan Thampuran, decided Thrissur should have its own festival. He invited the temples to gather at Vadakkunnathan instead. He organised them into two groups, led by the Paramekkavu and Thiruvambady temples. The two sides still try to outdo each other in every part of the festival.

sec.h: Hundreds of musicians under one tree
sec.t:
One of the most loved parts is the *Elanjithara melam*, a drum concert held under an old *elanji* tree in the temple grounds. Around 250 musicians play together, led by the *chenda*, a cylindrical drum beaten with sticks. Cymbals, horns and pipes join in.

The music begins slow and steady, then builds for hours, faster and faster. People in the crowd throw their arms in the air and keep time. The rhythm follows strict patterns that musicians spend years learning, and some performers have played at the festival for decades.

The day starts much earlier. From dawn, processions from the smaller temples arrive one after another, each with its own elephant and drummers, to pay respects at Vadakkunnathan. The one from Kanimangalam traditionally comes first. By the time the big melam begins, the city has been drumming for hours.

{{story:drums}}

In the late afternoon, the two teams line up facing each other. About 15 elephants stand on each side, decorated with gold-plated face coverings called *nettipattam*. On top of each sit riders holding fans, plumes and silk umbrellas.

Then the *kudamattam*, the exchange of umbrellas, begins. Each side raises a set of matching umbrellas, then swaps them for another, then another. Some are covered with sequins, some with lights, some with images of gods. Teams keep their designs secret for months. The crowd roars at each surprise.

sec.h: Fireworks and a promise to meet again
sec.t:
Before dawn, the night sky blazes with fireworks, known locally as *vedikettu*. The sound can be heard kilometres away. On the final day, the two teams' deities bid each other farewell, promising to meet again at next year's Pooram.

The festival also raises serious questions. Animal welfare groups worry about elephants standing in heat and crowds and about fireworks safety. Courts and the Kerala government have set rules on how long elephants can stand, how far crowds must stay back and how fireworks are stored. Festival organisers say they follow these rules carefully, and the debate continues.

People of many faiths join in, and Thrissur's shops and homes open their doors to visitors. Each elephant has a [[@people-mahouts|mahout]] who has often spent years with that one animal. The big drums of Pooram, chenda, maddalam and more, belong to an ancient family of instruments, the story of [[@drums|drums]]. And the bursts of colour in the morning sky come from metals burning in a clever way, explained in [[@fireworks|how fireworks work]].

text: Mysore Palace lights up because its royal family loved to show off a new wonder of the age: electric light. Its outline is covered in about 97,000 bulbs. When they all switch on together, every dome, arch and tower shines gold.

The lights come on for an hour on Sunday evenings and public holidays. During Dasara, the city's great autumn festival, they glow for two hours every night, and the whole city of [[@mysuru|Mysuru]] fills with visitors.
The palace was home to the Wodeyar family, who ruled the kingdom of Mysore for most of the past 600 years. It's now among the most visited places in India.

sec.t:
There has been a royal palace on this spot for centuries. The older one was made mostly of wood. In 1897, during the wedding of a princess, it caught fire and burned down.

The young maharaja's mother, who was ruling for him at the time, ordered a new palace in stone. The British architect Henry Irwin designed it, and it was finished in 1912. It is a three-storey building of grey granite, with marble domes and a tall central tower about 44 metres high.

Its style is called Indo-Saracenic. It mixes Hindu temple shapes, Mughal domes and arches, Rajput balconies and European glass and iron. Inside are halls with stained-glass ceilings, carved doors and floors of polished stone. Visitors take off their shoes before going inside.

sec.h: A city that took to electricity early

sec.t:
Today the bulbs run along every edge of the palace, like dots in a join-the-dots drawing. They trace the domes, the arches, the balconies and the tall central tower, so that after dark the whole outline of the building hangs in the air.

Keeping it working is a big job. Electricians check for fused bulbs and replace them, especially before Dasara. Many people say the best view is from the lawns in front, just as the lights come on and the crowd lets out a gasp.

Mysuru Dasara is the city's biggest festival, held over ten days around September or October. It celebrates the goddess Chamundeshwari's victory over the demon Mahishasura, who gave the city its name. Across India the same season brings Navaratri and [[@durga-puja|Durga Puja]].

On the last day, called Vijayadashami, a decorated [[@elephants-india|elephant]] carries a golden howdah, a seat said to weigh about 750 kg, holding an image of the goddess. It walks in a long procession called the Jamboo Savari, with bands, dancers and floats, from the palace through the city.

The Wodeyars ruled Mysore from the 1300s. In the 18th century, the general Hyder Ali and then his son [[@tipu-sultan|Tipu Sultan]] took power, until Tipu was killed fighting the British in 1799. The British then put the Wodeyars back on the throne.

After India's independence, Mysore joined India and the old kingdom became part of today's [[@karnataka|Karnataka]]. The palace is now run by the state government, though the royal family still lives in one part and still leads Dasara prayers inside.

text: The Seven Sisters are the seven states of India's northeast: Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur, [[@meghalaya|Meghalaya]], Mizoram, Nagaland and Tripura. The nickname was coined in 1972 by a journalist, Jyoti Prasad Saikia, who wrote about how closely these neighbours depend on one another. [[@sikkim|Sikkim]], which joined the region's official council in 2002, is often called their brother.

Together the states cover about 8% of [[@india-geography|India's land]] and hold about 4% of its people. They are linked to the rest of the country by the Siliguri Corridor, a narrow strip of land in West Bengal sometimes called the Chicken's Neck. Almost all of the region's border is with other countries.

sec.t:
The Northeast runs from the snowy eastern Himalayas in Arunachal Pradesh to the green hills of Mizoram. Through the middle flows the mighty [[@brahmaputra|Brahmaputra]]. In Assam it spreads so wide that it holds [[@majuli|Majuli]], one of the largest river islands in the world.

Meghalaya means "abode of the clouds". Its villages of Mawsynram and [[@india-wonder-cherrapunji|Cherrapunji]] are often called the [[@wettest-place|wettest places on Earth]], with more than 11 m of rain in some years. That is about six times the height of a tall adult. All that rain makes the region one of the greenest and richest in plants and animals anywhere in India.

In the Khasi and Jaintia hills of Meghalaya, streams turn into torrents in [[@monsoon|the monsoon]], and wooden bridges rot. So villagers grow bridges instead. They guide the roots of rubber fig trees across a stream, often along bamboo poles. Over 15 to 30 years, the roots thicken and knot together into a living bridge. Some are believed to be well over a century old, and one village has a double-decker bridge.

The Northeast is one of the most varied regions in the world. It is home to more than 200 communities, including the Assamese, Bodo, Khasi, Garo, Mizo, Meitei, Adi, Apatani and many Naga groups. Many speak languages related to those of Tibet and Southeast Asia rather than other Indian languages. That adds dozens of [[@languages-india|languages]] to India's count.

Festivals are just as varied. Assam celebrates [[@art-bihu|Bihu]], which marks the farming year. Nagaland holds the [[@india-wonder-hornbill-festival|Hornbill Festival]] every December, where tribes share dances, songs and food. Arunachal Pradesh's Dong village is among the first places in India to see the sunrise each morning.

For a long time the region felt far away to many Indians, and people from the Northeast have sometimes faced unfair stereotypes in other cities. New railways, roads and airports are bringing it closer. Today its music, football players, [[@mary-kom|boxers]] and food are known across the country.

text: Hundreds of English words come from Indian languages. Some you may use every day: *shampoo*, *pyjamas*, *bungalow*, *jungle*, *cot*, *loot* and *bandana*. Others belong to food and ideas: *chutney*, *curry*, *karma*, *guru* and *avatar*.

Most arrived during the 300 or so years when British traders, soldiers and officials lived in India. They picked up words from Hindi, Urdu, Bengali, Tamil, Persian and [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]] and carried them home. Some words changed meaning on the way. An *avatar*, in Hindu belief, is a god taking earthly form. Today it is also the little character that represents you in a video game.

sec.t:
*Pyjamas* comes from Persian and Urdu *pai jama*, "leg garment", loose trousers tied at the waist. British men in India adopted them for sleeping, and the habit travelled home. *Bandana* comes from the Hindi *bandhna*, "to tie", after a style of tie-dyed cloth. *Khaki*, from an Urdu word meaning "dusty", became the colour of army uniforms after British soldiers in India began dyeing their white clothes in the 1840s to hide the dirt.

A *bungalow* was originally a house "in the Bengal style", a single storey with a wide verandah. The word spread with the British across their empire and beyond, so you can now find bungalows in Bengaluru, London and Los Angeles. A *cot* comes from *khat*, a light wooden bed strung with rope.

sec.h: A massage that became a soap

sec.t:
*Jungle* comes from the Hindi *jangal*, which grew from the Sanskrit *jangala*, meaning dry, rough, uncultivated land. In English it came to mean almost the opposite: thick, wet forest. *Loot* is from Hindi *lut*, "plunder", and *thug* from *thag*, a cheat or robber.

*Juggernaut* comes from Jagannath, the deity of the great temple at Puri in Odisha. Each year, during the Rath Yatra festival, huge wooden [[@wheel-to-chariot|chariots]] carrying the deity are pulled through the streets by vast crowds of devotees. European visitors wrote about these giant chariots, and in English "juggernaut" came to mean any huge, unstoppable force.

In 1886, two British scholars, Henry Yule and Arthur Burnell, published a dictionary of Indian words used in English, with the odd title *Hobson-Jobson*. It listed well over a thousand words and is still fun to browse.

The flow hasn't stopped. [[@dictionaries|Dictionaries]] such as the Oxford English Dictionary keep adding Indian English words. In 2017 it added *jugaad*, a clever, low-cost fix. Food words travel fastest, as Indian restaurants spread around the world. A Mumbai [[@lunchbox-dabbawala|dabbawala]] or a plate of [[@biryani|biryani]] can now appear in a London newspaper without any explanation. That is how [[@english-spread|English]] has always grown, one borrowed word at a time.

text: Lemons are sour because their juice is full of acid, mostly citric acid. About 5 to 6 out of every 100 grams of lemon juice is citric acid. That makes it about as acidic as vinegar.
Your tongue has special cells for sourness. They notice acids by sensing tiny charged particles that acids release, and they send a sharp "sour" signal to your brain. That is the pucker you feel.

Oranges have citric acid too, but much less, and lots more sugar. So an orange tastes sweet, while a lemon makes your eyes water. Limes are about as sour as lemons, and a grapefruit sits somewhere in between.

st.reveal: Lemon and lime juice have roughly five times as much citric acid as orange juice. Oranges also pack far more sugar, which hides the sourness that is still there.
