sec.t:
A plant doesn't make fruit for fun. Fruit holds seeds, and the plant needs animals to eat the fruit and spread those seeds when the fruit is ready.

Many unripe fruits are sour or bitter, which puts animals off until the seeds are mature. As most fruits ripen, acid goes down and sugar goes up. Lemons are unusual: they keep much of their acid even when ripe. People like that sharpness, so farmers have picked and grown the sourest kinds for hundreds of years.

All citrus fruits are relatives. In 2018 scientists compared the genes of dozens of kinds and traced the family back to the foothills of the eastern Himalayas, around Assam, northern Myanmar and Yunnan in China. Wild citrus still grows in [[@northeast-india|northeast India]].

Many citrus fruits we eat are crosses. The lemon is a cross between the citron, a big bumpy fruit used in Indian pickles, and the bitter orange. The sweet orange is a mix of the pomelo and the mandarin.

India grows many of its own kinds. Assam has its long, fragrant Assam lemon, and Nagpur is so famous for its loose-skinned oranges that it is nicknamed Orange City. Florida and California are the big orange growers in the USA.

Citrus spread by trade. Arab traders took lemons around the Mediterranean, and Spanish sailors carried them to the Americas. Today India grows more lemons and limes than any other country, with Mexico not far behind.

{{story:history-of-medicine}}

For centuries, sailors on long voyages fell ill with scurvy. Their gums bled, their teeth loosened and old wounds opened up. Many died.

In 1747 a Scottish naval doctor named James Lind tried an experiment on a ship. He gave groups of sick sailors different treatments. The two who got oranges and lemons recovered fastest. Decades later, the British navy began handing out lemon juice, and later lime juice, to its sailors. That is how British sailors earned the American nickname "limeys".

We now know the cause. Scurvy comes from too little [[@vitamins|vitamin C]], which citrus fruit has plenty of. Your body can't make it, so it has to come from food.

Cooks use sourness to wake up a dish. A squeeze of lime lifts a plate of poha or a bowl of dal. In the USA, lemonade stands are a classic summer job for children, and key lime pie is a favourite in Florida.

Acid also keeps food from going bad, because many germs can't grow in it. That is one reason lemon and lime [[@pickles-achar|pickles]] can sit in a jar for months. And acid stops a cut apple from [[@food-science-apples-brown|browning]], which is why a few drops of lemon keep fruit salad looking fresh.

Our sense of sour is closely tied to [[@taste-why|taste]] and smell together. Bite a lemon with your nose pinched and it still tastes sour, but much of the lemony flavour vanishes.

text: Papad is a thin, crisp disc made from [[@lentils-world|lentil flour]]. Most often it's made from urad dal (black gram) flour, mixed with salt, spices like [[@cardamom-pepper|black pepper]] or cumin, and a little water to make a stiff dough. The dough is beaten, divided into small balls, and rolled out paper-thin. Then the discs are dried in the sun until hard.

Dry papad keeps for months. To eat it, you roast it over a flame, heat it in a microwave, or fry it in hot oil. It puffs, blisters and turns crisp in seconds. Papad is served with meals across India, from Rajasthani thalis to South Indian [[@south-indian-meals|banana-leaf meals]], where it's called appalam or pappadam.

st.prompt: Why does a papad puff and bubble when you roast it?

options.t: Tiny bits of water inside turn to steam and push the dough up
The heat makes the flour grow
Air from the room gets trapped under it

st.reveal: Even a dried papad has a little water left inside. When heated, that water turns to steam and makes small bubbles and blisters. The papad becomes light and crisp as the steam escapes.

sec.t:
Drying removes most of the water, so microbes can't grow. That's why papad lasts so long. On a hot, dry day, papads may dry in a few hours. In damp weather, it can take much longer.

Many families make a year's supply of papad in summer, when the sun is strong. Women in villages and towns often work together on rooftops and courtyards, rolling and drying hundreds of papads at once.

On 15 March 1959, seven women from Girgaum in [[@mumbai|Mumbai]] borrowed 80 rupees and began making papads on a rooftop. They wanted to earn money from home, using a skill they already had.

Their business became Shri Mahila Griha Udyog Lijjat Papad. It's a [[@cooperatives|cooperative]], which means the members own the business together and share its profits. Women join as members, often making papads at home and bringing them to a local branch.

Today Lijjat has tens of thousands of women members and branches across India. It has received national awards and is often held up as an example of women building a business on their own terms.

Even dry papad has a little water left inside. When heated, that water quickly turns to steam, pushing the dough up into bubbles and blisters. As the steam escapes, the papad becomes light and crunchy.

A [[@microwave|microwave]] heats the water inside the papad directly, so it puffs without any oil. Frying makes it puff more and taste richer, but it soaks up oil. Roasting over a flame gives a smoky, slightly charred taste.

Not all papad is made from urad dal. Moong dal papads are lighter. Rice papads are white and delicate. Sago papads puff up like clouds. Potato papads are a favourite in parts of North India.

Bikaner in Rajasthan is famous for spicy papads with black pepper. In the south, small, thick appalams are fried until puffed, then crushed over rice and rasam. In Gujarat, papad is sometimes cooked into a curry called papad nu shaak.

Indian restaurants in the UK and the USA often serve "poppadoms" with chutneys before a meal. The name comes from the South Indian pappadam. For many people abroad, it's their first taste of Indian food. It's a thin disc of lentil, dried in the sun, that started in Indian homes and rooftops.
